title: A Map In, a Pattern Out

scenes.visual: Title card: A Map In, a Pattern Out.

scenes.tts: Every smell starts as a map. In the mouse olfactory bulb, receptor neurons of one type converge on one glomerulus, so an odour lights up a fixed pattern of glomeruli. Piriform cortex does not keep that map. An odour switches on neurons scattered across the cortex. Yet the scattered pattern still knows which odours are chemically alike, and it can learn what an odour means. That is the change from bulb to cortex.
scenes.visual: A row of glomeruli with a few lit in a fixed pattern; arrows to a cortex sheet where scattered dots light up; two related odours give similar dot patterns; a small 'learned' tag appears.

Yet the scattered pattern still knows which odours are chemically alike, and it can learn what an odour means. That is the change from bulb to cortex.

scenes.tts: Stettler and Axel imaged piriform cortex in living mice. One odour activated neurons spread across the area, not gathered in a patch. Sosulski and colleagues then traced the output of a single glomerulus. In piriform cortex the axons spread diffusely. In the cortical amygdala, the same glomerulus made tidy patches. So the scattering belongs to piriform cortex, not to the whole bulb.
scenes.visual: Scattered lit cells on a piriform sheet; then one gold glomerulus with tracer, axons fanning evenly over piriform and forming separate patches in a cortical amygdala panel.

scenes.tts: Is chemistry lost in the scatter? Pashkovski and colleagues compared bulb inputs with piriform neurons. In both, related odours gave related population patterns, and the cortex grouped related odours more tightly than its input did. This is a map of similarity, not of place. Similar odours give similar patterns, wherever the cells sit.
scenes.visual: Two similarity grids side by side, bulb boutons and piriform; related odour pairs shaded; the piriform grid shows tighter clusters; a 'place' chip crossed out, a 'similarity' chip kept.

scenes.tts: Piriform neurons are wired to each other, and those connections are thought to store experience. Choi and colleagues made artificial ensembles with light. Paired with a reward, the mice learned one behaviour. Paired with a shock, they learned the opposite. So scattered activity can gain learned meaning. That is not the same as making the mice smell something.
scenes.visual: Recurrent links between scattered cortical cells; a light flash drives a subset; one branch to a water drop, one to a shock symbol; opposite arrows for approach and avoid; a nose icon with a question mark.

scenes.tts: The bulb shapes what the cortex receives. Granule cells and other interneurons trade signals with mitral and tufted cells through reciprocal synapses, giving recurrent and lateral inhibition. Timing matters too, though timing differences do not show which synapses made them. Sister cells that share one glomerulus had correlated average rates in anaesthetized mice, but fired at different moments in the breath. A shared address is not a shared message.
scenes.visual: Bulb schematic: glutamate arrow out, GABA arrow back at a dendrodendritic contact, inhibition spreading to a neighbour; then one breath cycle with spike ticks for two sister cells, same count, different phases.

scenes.tts: So the bulb hands over a map, and the cortex turns it into a scattered pattern that keeps chemical likeness and learns meaning. In mice, that pattern also drifts over weeks. What stays stable on top of a moving code is still an open question.
scenes.visual: Glomerular map on the left, arrow to the scattered cortical pattern on the right; the pattern shifts slightly frame to frame; a question mark over a 'stable readout' box.
